before_text: We re-tested the main claims of new robot-learning papers on an SO-101 arm with a Jetson Orin NX. The pieces cost €1,350 and the compute $45.10. Each re-test ran the cheapest baseline first, and its pass mark was committed before the run. Of the 37 paper claims we tested, 12 were valid on our hardware. Three proposed classes cover the failures: edge latency (a method misses the real-time budget on the edge GPU), zero-shot judges (a judge loses to a trivial signal) and latent planners (a planner loses to the commanded joints). A blind second reader still has to confirm the classes. We also verified our own pre-registration by commit history. For most gates the order of bar and result can be read from the repository, and for some it cannot.
after_text: 12 of the 37 paper claims we tested were valid on our hardware, an SO-101 arm with a Jetson Orin NX. The pieces cost €1,350 and the compute $45.10. For each claim we ran the cheapest baseline first and committed the pass mark before the test. The failures fall into three classes. Some methods miss the real-time budget on the edge GPU. Some zero-shot judges lose to a trivial signal. Some latent planners lose to the commanded joints. We propose these classes. A blind second reader has not confirmed them yet. We also read the commit history of our own gates. For most of them the bar comes before the result. For some the history does not show the order.

The ones missing from our papers mirror all belong to scheduled tests. One tested paper has no arXiv id and was not checked against a PDF.

before_text: Two works use the same arm to evaluate policies. A standardized real-world benchmark reports a taxonomy of failures and recoveries for VLA policies [arXiv:2606.08881]. A fleet of SO-101 cells evaluates policies at scale [arXiv:2607.24481]. The vla-eval tool runs VLAs across 14 simulation benchmarks [arXiv:2603.13966]. A benchmark of demonstration quality studies one method family [arXiv:2610.18869]. We test the claims behind methods (judges, world models, latency) against thresholds fixed before the run, and we audit our own pre-registration. RoboSeed [arXiv:2610.40026] is the closest work. It scores VLA and world-action models on five dimensions, including reproduction evidence and deployment affordability. Its reproduction-evidence score counts five audit milestones (configuration mapping, task records, task coverage, training records, seeds). Its authors state that this score is not a probability that a result is correct. We give one pass or fail per claim on a €1,350 rig.

before_text: LeWorldModel (LeWM) trains a world model in two parts. The encoder maps camera frames to a latent vector. The predictor takes the current latent and a sequence of actions and imagines the latents that follow. Both are trained together from pixels with a joint-embedding predictive (JEPA) loss. Papers built on these models propose several uses. Most of them need the predictor. One ranks a policy's candidate action chunks by their imagined outcome. Others flag a failure when the observed latent drifts from the predicted one, read the outcome of a grasp before it happens, or plan over several time scales. Each paper reports the use that worked on its own robot and data.
after_text: LeWorldModel (LeWM) trains a world model in two parts. The encoder maps camera frames to a latent vector. Most of the uses that later papers propose need the predictor. LeWM itself ranks a policy's candidate action chunks by their imagined outcome. ContactGuard reads the outcome of a grasp before it happens, HWM and H-JEPA plan over several time scales, and other papers flag a failure when the observed latent drifts from the predicted one. Each of these papers reports that its use worked on its own robot and data.

before_text: The controls came after the data. Each readout is a linear probe with leave-one-session-out (LOSO) cross-validation on the 69 rollouts (44 success, 25 failure, 13 sessions). The labels were given at rest by the author. The model was trained on teleoperation only and never saw these rollouts. No threshold was committed for these comparisons. That needs a day on the arm. All results come from one model at one data scale. A second point at 653 episodes is costed and queued. We did not run three controls. He stopped each run and labelled it at rest, not blind to the policy.

before_text: Robometer scales a general-purpose reward model through trajectory comparisons. TOPReward reads the token probabilities of a video-language model as hidden rewards. A survey of verifiers for robot policies covers the wider family. FAIL-Detect and SAFE learn uncertainty- and feature-based failure scores for imitation and VLA policies. FARM reads failure signals from the internal states of a frozen world model, like our world-model monitors. ReAP predicts action-conditioned risk, and our risk head follows it. VLA-Corrector verifies stages, Spotter adds a reflecting VLM, and REMORA tracks progress through errors and recovery. ArmnetBench and a standardized SO-101 VLA benchmark evaluate policies on the same arm. None of these works reports the elapsed-length baseline under the dataset's stopping rule.

before_text: We re-measured seven training-free methods for action chunking in flow-matching VLAs. Their papers report numbers from desktop GPUs. We ran them where a low-cost robot runs its policy, with SmolVLA on a Jetson Orin NX. All tests share one checkpoint and the same recorded episodes. Each test had its threshold committed before the run, and every number traces to a result file and a protocol commit. On this board the vision encoder takes 151.0 of 219.0 ms of server time per chunk (25 W). The two methods that act on the seam between chunks pass. A gradient-free prefix overwrite cuts the boundary jump by 72 % or more. Movement-primitive seam conditioning removes most of the seam jerk. The sampling methods do not transfer. vla.cpp samples in sequence, so every N-sample method pays for N chunks one after another.

before_text: Multiple training-free chunking tricks for flow-matching VLAs have come out this year. Their numbers always come from strong desktop or data-centre GPUs (RTX 4090, A100, H100, RTX 5090). On these, a chunk costs barely tens of milliseconds and spare compute is plentiful. A robot people can buy runs its policy on an edge GPU. There most of the chunk goes to the vision encoder, which these tricks don't affect. We measured how much of each trick is left on such a board.

before_text: Two tricks act on the seam between chunks, and both pass. The first overwrites the new chunk's executed prefix with the actions already committed. It passes the 50 % jump-cut bar at every delay, in PyTorch and in vla.cpp. In vla.cpp it adds 0.4 ms per chunk. The second is movement-primitive chunking [arXiv:2610.39451]. Projecting each chunk onto ten Gaussian bases keeps the error within its bar and removes within-chunk jerk. Conditioning on the last action sent removes 83–87 % of the seam jerk at +0.19° of error. Its paper reports 73–84 %. We measured on the commanded stream only.

before_text: Cutting the Euler steps from ten to two [arXiv:2610.32102] saves 41 ms per chunk at full power. The vision cost is much larger. The paper claims that the action cloud contracts around an unchanged centroid. It reports a cloud ratio of 0.51 on π0. Our ratio is 0.78. It falls between the bar of 0.70 and the fail line of 0.85, so the claim is not proven here. The paper also expects fewer steps to remove edge-GPU thermal throttling. Our Orin did not throttle at ten steps in either power mode. We keep ten steps, as the protocol says while the contraction is unproven.
